known_from_text.basis: Verses 1 and 4 address all the earth; verses 7–8 mention nations and peoples.
known_from_text.claim: The praise has a universal audience.

known_from_text.basis: Verse 6 describes the sea becoming dry ground and a river crossed on foot.
Verses 10–12 address God as the one who tested, refined, brought into a net, imposed affliction, caused people to ride over their heads, and brought them out.
known_from_text.claim: The community attributes both testing and deliverance to God.

known_from_text.basis: Verses 9–12 use “us” and “our”; verses 13–20 use first-person singular vows, distress, prayer, and testimony.
known_from_text.claim: The discourse moves from communal experience to individual commitment and testimony.

known_from_text.basis: Verses 13 and 15 specify burnt offerings; verse 15 names fattened animals, rams, cattle, and male goats.
known_from_text.claim: The offerings are concrete sacrificial acts in the Hebrew.

known_from_text.basis: Verse 19 explicitly affirms hearing and attention; verse 20 blesses God for not turning away prayer or steadfast kindness.
known_from_text.claim: The speaker affirms that God heard the prayer and did not withdraw kindness.

not_known_from_text.claim: David or another named person composed or spoke the psalm.
not_known_from_text.why_not: The heading contains no personal attribution, and the first-person speaker remains unnamed.

not_known_from_text.claim: The speaker was a king, priest, or identifiable historical individual.
not_known_from_text.why_not: Vow fulfillment and sacrifice do not specify the speaker's social or cultic office.

not_known_from_text.claim: The suffering describes one identifiable war, exile, or persecution.
not_known_from_text.why_not: The net, bodily oppression, fire, and water are not tied to named events, enemies, or dates.

not_known_from_text.claim: Verse 6 explicitly identifies the sea and river or dates the psalm to their crossing.
not_known_from_text.why_not: Neither body of water is named, and recollection of deliverance does not date composition.

not_known_from_text.claim: The individual testimony establishes that the speaker had never sinned.
not_known_from_text.why_not: Verse 18 concerns regarding wickedness in the heart and God's hearing; it does not assert lifelong sinlessness.

not_known_from_text.claim: The modern instruments, tempo, or section breaks reconstruct the ancient performance.
not_known_from_text.why_not: The Hebrew gives no such arrangement instructions, and Selah's precise performance function is not established by the supplied evidence.

guardrails.cultic_setting: God's house, payment of vows, burnt offerings, and named sacrificial animals in verses 13–15 imply sanctuary worship with actual sacrifice. The invitation to hear testimony in verse 16 gives the thanksgiving a public dimension. The English retains house, vows, offerings, and smoke but generalizes their sacrificial specificity. The text does not identify the speaker's office, a particular festival, or a securely dated ceremony.
guardrails.heading_attribution: The Hebrew heading says “For the director. A song. A psalm.” It supplies a performance designation and genre terms, but names no author, Davidic attribution, or historical occasion. The English omits this heading; its modern section labels supply no ancient attribution.

analyses.method: The audit compares the supplied Hebrew clauses, morphology, and token glosses with the English and the earlier full arrangement. Literal backbones preserve clause content and agency before evaluating compression, repetition, and added imagery. In verse 7, the supplied token list includes an exaltation verb absent from the displayed Hebrew line; the mismatched final glosses were not treated as translations of Selah. No external edition or lexicon was consulted.

sections.arc_note: Establishes the universal horizon and moves from commands to the prospect of worldwide worship. The opening chorus ends at the first Selah.
sections.theme: All the earth is summoned to acclaim God's glorious name and overwhelming deeds.
sections.title: Chorus

sections.arc_note: Moves from universal praise to remembered sea and river crossings, then warns rebels against self-exaltation. This section ends at Selah; the arrangement subsequently reprises verses 1–2.
sections.theme: An invitation to witness God's deliverance, enduring rule, and scrutiny of the nations.
sections.title: Verse 1

sections.arc_note: Verse 2 previews suffering and rescue; the bridge develops the trials and repeatedly celebrates relief. “Refine us” introduces a petition into the Hebrew's retrospective account. Combining these arrangement sections keeps their overlapping treatment of verses 10–12 within one continuous verse range.
sections.theme: Communal preservation through testing, oppression, fire, and water into abundance.
sections.title: Verse 2 + Bridge

sections.arc_note: The communal voice becomes an individual speaker at verse 13. The outro contains both the sacrificial commitment of verses 13–15 and the invitation to listen in verses 16–20. Guitar re-entry marks that internal turn, but the named section continues across Selah after verse 15. A closing reprise reconnects communal rescue with personal thanksgiving.
sections.theme: Personal fulfillment of vows, testimony to answered prayer, and blessing for enduring kindness.
sections.title: Outro

analyses.summary: The setting follows the psalm from worldwide praise through remembered deliverance and communal suffering to personal vows, testimony, and blessing. Its driving rock arrangement and repeated deliverance refrain emphasize survival and relief. Poetic expansions make the language bodily and immediate, especially “Into room to breathe.” The principal losses are the specific sacrificial vocabulary, God's explicit agency in allowing oppression in verse 12, and the explicit description of the testimony as what God did for the speaker in verse 16. Selah is not sung, and the Hebrew superscription is omitted.
